title: Lettre Tate (mai 66) (Cristaux) : lettre (1966), tapuscrit (s.d.), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the 1966 letter to Tate on crystals. The page begins by finishing §1.15 and then covers §1.16.

(i) End of 1.15. A 'bicrystal of weight i' over an arbitrary base S, possibly over Z, is a crystal of modules M on S. For every prime p, the restriction M_p to the fibre S_p = V(p·O_S) carries Frobenius and Verschiebung maps F_p, V_p. When S is of finite type over Z and dominates Spec Z, Grothendieck remarks that the family (F_p) behaves like a system of arithmetic Frobenii. In weight 1 (Dieudonné-type objects), the crystal with this extra structure 'ties together' the formal groups it produces in the various characteristics.

(ii) 1.16 'Un retour en arrière', a self-correction of the earlier sections:
- The test category C in 1.0/1.1 should not consist of R-thickenings S→T of all of S. It should consist of R-morphisms U→T, with U an open subscheme of S and U→T a nilpotent closed immersion.
- The definition is only sensible ('n'est guère raisonnable que si') when the fibred category F is a Zariski stack over (Sch)/R, meaning objects and arrows glue.
- Gluing is needed to define inverse images in 1.3. The construction given there (via an amalgamated sum) works only for affine S, S'. In general one localises, since otherwise the pushout can fall outside the category of preschemes.

(iii) He then introduces the 'site cristallogène de S sur R':
- Objects are pairs (U open in S, U→T a surjective closed R-immersion defined by a nilpotent ideal).
- The topology is Zariski: an open cover (T_i) of T induces the covering (U∩T_i → T_i).
- A sheaf is a family of Zariski sheaves F_{U→T} on each T. Each arrow (U→T)→(U'→T') gives a transition map from the inverse image of F_{U'→T'} to F_{U→T}. This map need not be an isomorphism; a handwritten addition says it is one when T→T' is an open immersion.
- 'In particular, associating…' leads to the structure sheaf O_C on the next page. There, crystals of quasi-coherent modules become the quasi-coherent O_C-modules, i.e. crystals are the sheaves whose transition maps are all isomorphisms.

In modern terms this is the (nilpotent) infinitesimal site/topos of S/R, before divided powers were added. The next page's marginal note says it works in characteristic 0 but not in characteristic p, for lack of divided powers; that gap is what Berthelot's crystalline site fills.
errors: Not an error but a self-acknowledged defect: the earlier definitions 1.1/1.3 are wrong globally. The page corrects them by allowing U to be an open of S and by requiring F to be a Zariski stack.

Implicit gap, recognised on the next page: without divided-power structures, cohomology of this nilpotent site does not give de Rham cohomology in characteristic p. The site described here is the infinitesimal site, which is correct only in characteristic 0.
Wording 'n'est guère raisonnable alors que si' is a slip for 'n'est guère raisonnable que si' (only if).

ideas.what: Site whose objects are nilpotent thickenings U→T of opens U of S over R, with the Zariski topology. Sheaves are systems F_T with not-necessarily-invertible transition maps; crystals are the sheaves with invertible transition maps.
ideas.modern_name: infinitesimal (nilpotent) site / topos; prototype of the crystalline site
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes, IHES 1966, in Dix exposés 1968); divided-power version by Berthelot (1974)
ideas.where_published: Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes (Dix exposés sur la cohomologie des schémas, 1968); the Tate letter itself is known and cited in the literature

ideas.what: Crystals defined via a fibred category require a Zariski stack condition; inverse image is first defined for affines and then extended by localisation.
ideas.modern_name: stack condition / descent for crystals; local definition of pullback
ideas.where_published: Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes (1968)

ideas.what: Bicrystals over an arbitrary base: a crystal on S/Z with an F_p, V_p structure on each characteristic-p fibre. This relates the formal groups in different characteristics through one global object.
ideas.modern_name: global/arithmetic F-crystals with Frobenius at all primes; cf. Frobenius lifts at all primes (Λ-structures), Fontaine–Laffaille / Fontaine–Messing type families
ideas.usually_credited_to: no single standard attribution; related to Borger's Λ-geometry and 'Frobenius at every p' philosophies
ideas.where_published: Tate letter (May 1966); unsure whether it appears elsewhere

missed.claim: Grothendieck proposes one global crystal over a Z-scheme carrying a Frobenius/Verschiebung structure at every prime simultaneously, read as 'arithmetic Frobenii', to tie together formal groups in all characteristics. This prefigures global objects with Frobenius structure at all primes (Λ-ring / Borger-style 'Frobenius at every p' geometry, global Dieudonné-type data). The literature developed this mostly prime-by-prime, though the idea is in the (known) Tate letter.
missed.quote: les différents F_p jouant le rôle d'homomorphismes de frobenius ... le cristal avec sa bi-structure supplémentaire permet de relier entre eux les groupes formels en les diverses caractéristiques
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Global, all-primes Frobenius structures are of current interest (Λ-rings, prismatic/absolute cohomology over Z). An explicit early formulation by Grothendieck is a modest historical antecedent, but it is only a sketch.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a self-correction and introduces the infinitesimal ('cristallogène') site, which is well known from the Tate letter and the 1966 IHES lectures. The only slightly underexplored point is the all-primes bicrystal over Z, which is a sketch rather than a result.
transcription_corrections: 'le sorite 1.3' appears typed over a mistyped word ('sortie'/'sortite'); read 'sorite'.
'dans 1.0.' is typed over a different character; read '1.0'.
'R-' is a handwritten insertion before 'flèches S→T'.
The handwritten 'C' above 'est' gives 'sous-jacente C est celle des...'.
In 'sur les buts des objets de C', 'buts' is struck and 'objets,' written above. This yields 'sur les objets des objets de C', i.e. the schemes T. The comma after 'avec' is handwritten.
The full handwritten line at the bottom reads '(et qui est un isom si T→T' est une imm. ouverte)', inserted after 'isomorphisme !)'.
Handwritten page numbers: '15' at top right and '16' at bottom left.
